stem: What is the basis of classification of algae?
solution:
Algae are classified mainly on the basis of the **type of pigment** they possess and the **type of stored food**. The **cell wall** composition, the **number and position of flagella** and the **habitat** are also used. On this basis algae are divided into three classes: **Chlorophyceae**, **Phaeophyceae** and **Rhodophyceae**.

| Basis | Chlorophyceae (green algae) | Phaeophyceae (brown algae) | Rhodophyceae (red algae) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Major pigments | Chlorophyll a, b | Chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin | Chlorophyll a, d, phycoerythrin |
| Stored food | Starch | Mannitol, laminarin | Floridean starch |
| Cell wall | Cellulose | Cellulose and algin | Cellulose, pectin and poly sulphate esters |
| Flagella (number and position) | 2-8, equal, apical | 2, unequal, lateral | Absent |
| Habitat | Fresh water, brackish water, salt water | Fresh water (rare), brackish water, salt water | Fresh water (some), brackish water, salt water (most) |
groundedIn: §3.1; §3.1.1; §3.1.2; §3.1.3; Table 3.1 — algae divided into Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae; pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella of each class in the class sections and Table 3.1 (flagella 2-8 apical and the habitat column)

stem: When and where does reduction division take place in the life cycle of a liverwort, a moss, a fern, a gymnosperm and an angiosperm?
solution:
In all five, **reduction division (meiosis)** takes place in the **sporophyte**, at the time of **spore formation**, and produces haploid spores. The zygote itself does not undergo reduction division.

| Plant | When | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Liverwort (e.g. Marchantia) | During spore formation in the sporophyte; the zygote first grows into a sporophyte | In the **capsule** of the sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule), which stays attached to the gametophyte |
| Moss (e.g. Funaria) | During spore formation in the sporophyte | In the **capsule** of the sporophyte |
| Fern | During spore formation | In the **spore mother cells** of the **sporangia** borne on sporophylls of the sporophyte |
| Gymnosperm (e.g. Pinus) | During formation of microspores and megaspores | In the **microsporangia** on microsporophylls of the male cones (microspores); in the **megaspore mother cell** of the nucellus of the **ovule** (megasporangium), which forms four megaspores |
| Angiosperm | During formation of pollen grains and megaspores | In the **microsporangia** of the flower (forming pollen grains) and in the megaspore mother cell of the **ovule** inside the flower |
groundedIn: §3.2; §3.2.1; §3.2.2; §3.3; §3.4; §3.5 — bryophyte zygotes do not undergo reduction division immediately, sporophyte cells undergo meiosis; liverwort and moss spores formed after meiosis in the capsule; fern sporangia produce spores by meiosis in spore mother cells; gymnosperm megaspore mother cell in the nucellus divides meiotically, microspores in microsporangia; angiosperm pollen grains and ovules develop in flowers; BEYOND CHAPTER: meiosis in the microsporangia (pollen mother cells) and in the megaspore mother cell of the ovule

stem: Name three groups of plants that bear archegonia. Briefly describe the life cycle of any one of them.
solution:
**Bryophytes**, **pteridophytes** and **gymnosperms** bear archegonia.

**Life cycle of a pteridophyte (fern):**

1. The main plant body is the diploid **sporophyte**, differentiated into true root, stem and leaves with well-differentiated vascular tissues. It is the dominant phase.
2. The sporophyte bears **sporangia** subtended by leaf-like appendages called **sporophylls**; in some (Selaginella, Equisetum) the sporophylls form compact **strobili** or cones.
3. **Spore mother cells** in the sporangia undergo **meiosis** to produce haploid **spores**.
4. The spores germinate into small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophytes called **prothallus**, which need cool, damp, shady places to grow.
5. The prothallus bears the male sex organs (**antheridia**) and female sex organs (**archegonia**).
6. **Water** is required to carry the **antherozoids** released from the antheridia to the mouth of the archegonium.
7. A male gamete fuses with the egg in the archegonium to form the diploid **zygote**.
8. The zygote produces a multicellular, well-differentiated sporophyte, and the cycle is repeated.
groundedIn: §3.2; §3.3; §3.4; Fig. 3.3 — archegonia in bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms; pteridophyte sporophyte, sporophylls and strobili, spores by meiosis, prothallus, antheridia and archegonia, water for fertilisation, zygote to sporophyte

stem: Mention the ploidy of the following: protonemal cell of a moss; primary endosperm nucleus in dicot, leaf cell of a moss; prothallus cell of a ferm; gemma cell in Marchantia; meristem cell of monocot, ovum of a liverwort, and zygote of a fern.
solution:
| Cell | Ploidy | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Protonemal cell of a moss | **Haploid (n)** | The protonema develops directly from a haploid spore; it is the first stage of the gametophyte |
| Primary endosperm nucleus in dicot | **Triploid (3n)** | It is formed by the fusion of a male gamete with two haploid polar nuclei |
| Leaf cell of a moss | **Haploid (n)** | The leafy stage is part of the gametophyte |
| Prothallus cell of a fern | **Haploid (n)** | The prothallus is the gametophyte formed from a spore |
| Gemma cell in Marchantia | **Haploid (n)** | Gemmae are asexual buds formed in gemma cups on the haploid thallus (gametophyte) |
| Meristem cell of monocot | **Diploid (2n)** | The angiosperm plant body is the sporophyte |
| Ovum of a liverwort | **Haploid (n)** | It is produced in the archegonium of the haploid gametophyte |
| Zygote of a fern | **Diploid (2n)** | It is formed by the fusion of a male gamete with the egg |

The book prints "ferm"; it means fern.
groundedIn: §3.2; §3.2.1; §3.2.2; §3.3; §3.5 — bryophyte plant body haploid gametophyte, protonema develops from a spore, gemmae on the thalli; prothallus gametophyte from spores, zygote from fusion of gametes; angiosperm plant body; BEYOND CHAPTER: primary endosperm nucleus is triploid (3n), from a male gamete and two polar nuclei

stem: Write a note on economic importance of algae and gymnosperms.
solution:
**Economic importance of algae:**

1. At least **half of the total carbon dioxide fixation** on earth is carried out by algae through photosynthesis.
2. Being photosynthetic, they increase the level of **dissolved oxygen** in their immediate environment.
3. They are **primary producers** of energy-rich compounds, which form the basis of the food cycles of all aquatic animals.
4. **Food:** about 70 species of marine algae are used as food, e.g. species of Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum.
5. **Hydrocolloids:** marine brown and red algae produce water-holding substances used commercially, e.g. **algin** (brown algae) and **carrageen** (red algae).
6. **Agar**, obtained from Gelidium and Gracilaria, is used to grow microbes and in preparing ice-creams and jellies.
7. **Chlorella**, a unicellular alga rich in proteins, is used as a **food supplement**, even by space travellers.

**Economic importance of gymnosperms:**

1. **Timber:** tall trees such as Pinus and Cedrus yield softwood timber used in construction, furniture and paper pulp.
2. **Resin and turpentine** are obtained from Pinus.
3. The seeds of some pines are **edible** (chilgoza).
4. Cycas, Pinus and Ginkgo are grown as **ornamentals**.
5. The coralloid roots of Cycas are associated with \(\text{N}_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria.
groundedIn: §3.1; §3.4; Fig. 3.4 — algae: half of CO2 fixation, dissolved oxygen, primary producers, 70 food species, algin and carrageen, agar from Gelidium and Gracilaria, Chlorella; gymnosperms: Pinus, Cedrus, Cycas, Ginkgo and Cycas coralloid roots; BEYOND CHAPTER: timber from Pinus and Cedrus, resin and turpentine, chilgoza seeds, ornamental use

stem: Both gymnosperms and angiosperms bear seeds, then why are they classified separately?
solution:
Both bear seeds, but they are classified separately because in **gymnosperms the ovules are naked**: they are not enclosed by any ovary wall and the seeds remain uncovered, whereas in **angiosperms** the pollen grains and ovules develop in **flowers** and the **seeds are enclosed in fruits**.

| Basis of difference | Gymnosperms | Angiosperms |
|---|---|---|
| Ovules | Naked, not enclosed by an ovary wall, exposed before and after fertilisation | Develop in specialised structures called flowers |
| Seeds | Naked (uncovered) | Enclosed in fruits |
| Flowers | Absent; sporophylls form male and female cones (strobili) | Present |
| Fruits | Absent | Present |
| Examples | Cycas, Pinus, Ginkgo | Wolffia, Eucalyptus |
groundedIn: §3.4; §3.5 — gymnosperm ovules not enclosed by any ovary wall, seeds not covered, sporophylls form cones; angiosperm pollen grains and ovules in flowers, seeds enclosed in fruits, Wolffia to Eucalyptus

stem: What is heterospory? Briefly comment on its significance. Give two examples.
solution:
**Heterospory** is the production of two kinds of spores, large **megaspores (macrospores)** and small **microspores**, by the same plant.

**Significance:**

1. The megaspores and microspores germinate into **female** and **male gametophytes** respectively.
2. The female gametophyte is **retained on the parent sporophyte** for variable periods.
3. The zygote develops into a young **embryo within the female gametophyte**.
4. This event is a **precursor to the seed habit**, considered an important step in evolution. In gymnosperms, which are heterosporous, the megaspore develops into the female gametophyte inside the ovule, and the ovule becomes the seed.

**Examples:** Selaginella and Salvinia (pteridophytes). All gymnosperms, such as Cycas and Pinus, are also heterosporous.
groundedIn: §3.3; §3.4 — Selaginella and Salvinia produce macro and micro spores; female gametophyte retained on the sporophyte, embryo develops within it, precursor to the seed habit; gymnosperms are heterosporous, megaspore develops into female gametophyte within the ovule

context: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples:-
solution: **Protonema** is the first stage of the gametophyte of a moss, which develops directly from a spore. It is a creeping, green, branched and frequently filamentous stage. The second, leafy stage develops from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud. Example: mosses such as Funaria and Polytrichum.
groundedIn: §3.2.2 — the protonema stage develops directly from a spore; creeping, green, branched, frequently filamentous; leafy stage from secondary protonema; Funaria, Polytrichum

context: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples:-
solution: **Antheridium** is the multicellular **male sex organ** of bryophytes and pteridophytes. In bryophytes it produces **biflagellate antherozoids** (male gametes). Examples: the antheridia borne on the antheridiophore of the male thallus of Marchantia, at the apex of the leafy shoots of mosses, and on the prothallus of ferns.
groundedIn: §3.2; §3.2.2; §3.3; Fig. 3.2 — male sex organ called antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids; Marchantia male thallus with antheridiophore; moss sex organs at apex of leafy shoots; antheridia on pteridophyte gametophytes

context: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples:-
solution: **Archegonium** is the multicellular, **flask-shaped female sex organ** that produces a **single egg**. Fertilisation takes place inside it. It occurs in bryophytes (e.g. Marchantia, borne on the archegoniophore of the female thallus), pteridophytes (on the prothallus of ferns) and gymnosperms (the female gametophyte of Pinus bears two or more archegonia).
groundedIn: §3.2; §3.3; §3.4; Fig. 3.2 — archegonium is flask-shaped and produces a single egg; Marchantia female thallus with archegoniophore; archegonia on pteridophyte gametophytes; gymnosperm female gametophyte bears two or more archegonia

context: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples:-
solution: **Diplontic** describes a life cycle in which the **diploid sporophyte** is the dominant, photosynthetic, independent plant body and the gametophyte is highly reduced and depends on it. Example: gymnosperms such as Pinus and Cycas. Their male gametophyte (the pollen grain) is confined to a limited number of cells, and the female gametophyte is retained within the megasporangium; neither has an independent free-living existence.
groundedIn: §3.4 — gymnosperm male gametophyte highly reduced and confined to a limited number of cells (pollen grain); female gametophyte retained within megasporangium; gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence; BEYOND CHAPTER: the term diplontic (dominant diploid sporophyte, reduced gametophyte)

context: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples:-
solution: **Sporophylls** are **leaf-like appendages** that bear or subtend **sporangia**. In some pteridophytes they form distinct compact structures called **strobili** or cones, e.g. Selaginella and Equisetum. In gymnosperms, microsporophylls and megasporophylls are arranged spirally on an axis to form male and female cones, e.g. Pinus.
groundedIn: §3.3; §3.4; Fig. 3.3 — sporangia subtended by leaf-like appendages called sporophylls, forming strobili in Selaginella and Equisetum; gymnosperm sporophylls arranged spirally to form male and female cones

context: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples:-
solution: **Isogamy** is sexual reproduction by the fusion of two gametes that are **similar in size**. The gametes may be flagellated, as in **Ulothrix**, or non-flagellated (non-motile), as in **Spirogyra**.
groundedIn: §3.1 — gametes flagellated and similar in size (Ulothrix) or non-flagellated but similar in size (Spirogyra); such reproduction is called isogamous

stem: Describe the important characteristics of gymnosperms.
solution:
**Gymnosperms** (gymnos: naked, sperma: seeds) are plants in which the **ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall** and remain exposed before and after fertilisation, so the **seeds are naked**. Their important characteristics are:

1. **Habit:** medium-sized or tall trees and shrubs; the giant redwood **Sequoia** is one of the tallest tree species.
2. **Roots:** generally tap roots. Pinus roots have a fungal association (**mycorrhiza**); Cycas has small specialised **coralloid roots** associated with \(\text{N}_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria.
3. **Stems:** unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus).
4. **Leaves:** simple or compound, adapted to withstand extremes of temperature, humidity and wind. Conifers have **needle-like leaves** with a thick cuticle and **sunken stomata** that reduce water loss.
5. **Heterosporous:** they produce haploid **microspores** and **megaspores** in sporangia borne on **sporophylls**, which are arranged spirally to form male and female **strobili (cones)**.
6. **Male gametophyte:** highly reduced, confined to a few cells; it is the **pollen grain**, developed within the microsporangia.
7. **Ovule:** the megaspore mother cell differentiates from a cell of the nucellus, which is protected by envelopes. It divides meiotically to form four megaspores; one develops into the multicellular **female gametophyte** bearing two or more **archegonia**.
8. The gametophytes have **no independent free-living existence**; they remain within the sporangia on the sporophyte.
9. The pollen grains are carried in **air currents** to the opening of the ovules; the **pollen tube** carries the male gametes to the archegonia and discharges them near their mouth.
10. After fertilisation the zygote develops into an embryo and the ovules into **seeds**, which are not covered. Cones are on the same tree in Pinus, but on different trees in Cycas.
groundedIn: §3.4; Fig. 3.4 — ovules not enclosed by ovary wall, naked seeds; Sequoia; tap roots, mycorrhiza in Pinus, coralloid roots in Cycas; leaf adaptations; heterosporous with spirally arranged sporophylls forming cones; pollen grain; ovule and female gametophyte with archegonia; gametophytes not free-living; pollen carried in air currents and pollen tube; seeds not covered
